text:
Verses 29–35

These verses command the Muslims to fight the People of the Book so that they pay the tribute (jizya); they also mention different aspects of how the People of the Book have strayed from the truth in both belief and practice.

(9:29) Fight those who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day, nor forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor practise the religion of truth, from among those who were given the Book, until they pay the tribute out of hand, being humbled.

Based on numerous Qur’anic verses, the People of the Book (or Ahl al-Kitāb) are the Jews and the Christians, as are the Zoroastrians, according to the verse: Indeed the faithful, the Jews, the Sabaeans, the Christians, the M agians and the polytheists—Allah will indeed judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed Allah is witness to all things (22:17). This is because the verse enumerates all of the heavenly religions1 in contrast to the idolaters. As we have already mentioned, the Sabeans were a sect of Zoroastrians who were influenced by Judaism and adopted a syncretic system of beliefs based on both traditions.

The context of the verse indicates that the word ‘from’ (min) in the phrase ‘from among those who were given the Book’ is used for exposition (bayān) rather than division (tabʿīḍ).2 This is because the Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians

1 In other words, heavenly revelations and it should not be misconstrued to mean “different religions”. (Pub.)

2 In other words, ‘from among those who were given the Book’ does not mean that there is a group within the People of the Book who ‘do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day, nor forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor practise the religion of truth,’ which is what would be implied if ‘from’ was used are each single communities of faith like the M uslims, even if they have divided into different branches, split into different sects, and intermingled with one another. If, on the other hand, the verse had meant to say that only some of the People of the Book were to be fought while all of them were required to pay tribute, or that only those of them who were to be fought should pay the tribute, the verse would have needed to include further explanation to convey this meaning.

When God says, from among those who were given the Book, this is an exposition of the phrase immediately before it, those who do not have faith in Allah. Therefore, the descriptions given in the verse apply to the entirety of the People of the Book.

There are three attributes God singles out for mention here: They do not believe in God or the Last Day, they do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and they do not follow the religion of truth. As for the first attribute, those who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day, how can this be reconciled with what God has said elsewhere in the Qur’an? For example, He describes the Jews and Christians as ‘People of the Book,’ which means they believe in a holy book that has been sent down from God to one of His messengers. Then, there are hundreds of verses in the Qur’an which quote them either affirming their belief in God or saying things that show they believe in God.

Equally, there are verses which show they believed in the Last Day as well. For instance: And they say, ‘The Fire shall not touch us except for a number of days’ (2:80); or: And they say, ‘No one shall enter paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian’ (2:111).

However, God does not distinguish in the Qur’an between believing in Him and believing in the Last Day, for denying the Last Day means denying God and denying God means denying the Last Day. Likewise, He says that anyone who distinguishes between believing in Him and His messengers, believing in one but not the other, is also a disbeliever: Those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and seek to separate Allah from His messengers, and say, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in some’ and seek to take a way in between, it is they who are truly faithless, and W e have prepared for the faithless

a humiliating punishment (4:150–1).

Therefore, because the People of the Book do not believe in the to signify division. Instead, because it is expository, it means that this description

refers to all the People of the Book, as Ṭabāṭabāʾī elaborates below. (Trans.) prophethood of M uḥammad, they are, in fact, disbelievers, even if they believe in God and the Last Day. Note that the Qur’an does not say that they denied one of God’s signs, namely prophethood, rather it says that they disbelieved in God and the Last Day, just as the idolaters are classed as disbelievers in God because they were not monotheists, even if they accepted the existence of a supreme deity.

So, even while they affirm the Creator and the Resurrection, they do so in a way that does not fully accord with the truth. For example, by saying that Jesus is the Son of God, or that Ezra is the Son of God, they are akin to the idolaters and polytheists who say that there is a deity that is the parent of other deities. Similar to this is the belief of the Jews that they will only be punished for a short time and the belief of the Christians that Christ’s sacrifice has absolved them of their sins.

Therefore, when God says that the People of the Book do not believe in Him or the Last Day, it appears that this is because they do not perceive the truths of monotheism and the Resurrection, even if they affirm their belief in God. This is because, according to the Qur’an’s own account, some of them espouse doctrines that contradict God’s divinity or contradict the Resurrection (although the Torah today does not contain any mention of the Resurrection whatsoever).

The second attribute assigned to them in this verse is that they do not forbid what Allah and His M essenger have forbidden. This refers to the things that the Jews consider permissible that the Qur’an enumerates in Sūrah alBaqarah, Sūrah al-Nisāʾ, and elsewhere, or that the Christians consider wine and the flesh of swine permissible even though they are both forbidden in the teachings of Moses, Jesus, and M uḥammad and their embezzling people’s wealth falsely, of which they are accused in the subsequent verse: Indeed many of the scribes and monks wrongfully eat up the people’s wealth (9:34). The word messenger (rasūl) in the phrase nor forbid what Allah and His M essenger have forbidden could refer to their own messengers who they accept, such as M oses for the Jews and Jesus for the Christians. In this case, it means that each of the two nations does not forbid itself what their own messenger forbade them, even though they recognise him as a messenger and affirm their belief in the truth of his message. And this is an act of brazen disrespect for God and His messenger and an example of their treating the truth like a plaything.

Alternatively, ‘messenger’ could refer to the Prophet M uḥammad, whose mission they find prophesied in their own scriptures, the Torah and the Evangel, and who permits them all good things, forbids them only from uncleanliness, and removes the shackles and fetters that were upon them. In this case, the Qur’an calls attention to their failure to forbid what God and His M essenger had declared forbidden in order to reprimand and criticise them. It is also to encourage the faithful to fight against them for disregarding what God and His Messenger had forbidden in their religion and for disrespecting God’s boundaries.

This second reading is perhaps supported by the fact that if, when God said ‘messenger,’ he meant the messenger of each nation, such as Moses for the Jews and Jesus for the Christians, then it would have been more befitting to say, ‘They do not forbid what God and His messengers forbade,’ which is the habit of the Qur’an in such contexts, because this points to the multitude of messengers. For example, see the following verses:

They… seek to separate Allah from His messengers (4:150)

Their messengers said, ‘Is there any doubt about Allah…?’ (14:10)

Their messengers brought them manifest proofs (10:13).

Because the Christians rejected the prohibitions of the Torah and the Evangel, they did not forbid what either Moses or Jesus had forbidden, and if this is what is meant by the verse then it would not be correct to say that they did not forbid what Allah and His Messenger (singular) have forbidden. Moreover, when one reflects on the general aims of Islam, they will have no doubt that the ordinance to fight the People of the Book until they pay tribute (jizya) was not revealed to bring worldly benefit to the Muslims and their allies or so that they could live lives of luxury and enjoyment in the manner of the kings and noblemen of different nations. On the contrary, the goal

of the religion is to make truth, justice, and piety triumph over falsehood, tyranny, and immorality. This is so that people will not be distracted by transitory desires on their journey towards God, so they can receive a beneficial

moral education without being led astray by false teachings, and so they do not find themselves being pulled in different directions. Otherwise, the human order would collapse. Of course, if one or more people do not want to receive the teachings of Islam, then they should be allowed to be free to choose their own religion, so long as it is a religion of monotheism, such as Judaism, Christianity, or Zoroastrianism, and so long as they do not oppose Islam openly. This shows the utmost justice and fairness of the religion of truth that triumphs over all others.

As for the tribute—or jizya—this is a monetary tax taken from them in return for maintaining their protected status—or dhimma—and to look after their needs, and this sort of taxation is something no government can do without, whether it is based on truth or falsehood.

From the above explanation, it is evident that what is meant by these forbidden things are those things forbidden in Islam, which God has determined should not be allowed to spread within global Islamic society, and what

is meant by the religion of truth (dīn al-ḥaqq) is the teachings that God has determined should be followed in that society.

Therefore, these forbidden things are those that have been forbidden by God and His Messenger Muḥammad, who brought the message of Islam to the world, and the three attributes that are mentioned in the verse— who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day, and so on—are intended explain the rationale for fighting the People of the Book.

This, in turn, demonstrates the error of those who argue: ‘It is irrational for the People of the Book to forbid themselves those things that God and His M essenger have forbidden to us, unless they embrace Islam, as this verse is about the People of the Book, not sinful Muslims.’

The answer to this argument is that the goal of fighting them is not that they forbid what Islam has forbidden while still following their own religion, rather it is that they do not openly do things that Islam has forbidden in society without there being some barrier to prevent these spreading or to prevent others from doing them without restraint, such as openly drinking wine, eating

the flesh of swine, embezzling the money of others. Therefore, the purpose of fighting them is so that they come under Islam’s protection (dhimma) and do not openly perform such acts in public. This means that the evil of these acts is contained amongst themselves only.

Perhaps this is what the verse means when it says they should pay the tribute out of hand, being humbled (wa hum ṣāghirūn), as we will discuss when

we come to the end of the verse.

The third attribute of theirs that God highlights is that they do not practise the religion of truth, meaning they do not take it as their own religion or

way of life.

However, the possessive construct, dīn al-ḥaqq (lit. ‘religion of truth’), is not a case of placing a noun in a possessive construct with its adjective, which would render the meaning ‘the religion of truth.’ On the contrary, this is a literal possessive construct, meaning the religion that belongs to the truth, because it embodies the truth that God has decreed for humankind and propels them towards it; it guides people to the truth and those who follow it reach

the truth. Therefore, the phrase ‘religion of truth’ is similar in meaning to ‘the path of truth’ (ṭarīq al-ḥaqq) or ‘the path of error’ (ṭarīq al-ḍalāl) in the sense that these are routes that lead to truth or error, meaning that the destination of the former path is the truth, while the destination of the latter is error. This meaning can be grasped form other verses of the Qur’an, such as: So set your countenance upon the religion as a people of pure faith, the origination of

Allah according to which He originated mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation; that is the upright religion, but most people do not know (30:30); and: Indeed, with Allah religion is Islam (3:19). These and other verses like them all affirm that the teachings of this religion are rooted in the fundamental realities of the cosmos, which the Prophet calls people towards and bids them to follow. Adopting these teachings as a way of life is called ‘submission to God’ (islām lillāh). Therefore, the Prophet is calling humanity to something that they have no excuse not to accept and submit to, namely following the practical moral programme towards which the very realities of the cosmos point. Or, to put it another way, submitting to God’s moral will (al-irādā al-tashrīʿiyya) stems from submitting to his cosmic will (al-irāda al-takwīniyya).

In short, objective reality has a religion and a way of life that emanates from it and calls people towards it just as falsehood and error have a religion that they call towards. The former is following the truth, while the latter is following one’s own desires: Had the Truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have surely fallen apart (23:71).

Therefore, when we refer to Islam as ‘the religion of truth’ (dīn al-ḥaqq), this means that its teachings are rooted in the cosmic order, that its path corresponds with the realities of creation, and that we are drawn towards it by the

God-given nature (fiṭra), with which all human beings are endowed. There is no altering Allah’s creation; that is the upright religion.

From the above, we can conclude the following:

Firstly, that when the Qur’an says the People of the Book do not believe in God or the Last Day, this means they have not adopted the faith that is acceptable to God; when it says they do not forbid what God and His Messenger

have forbidden, this means they do not care about openly committing sins that are harmful to human society and that undermine the efforts of the government of truth that rules over it; and when it says they do not follow the

religion of truth, this means that they do not follow the true way of life that is in harmony with both their own God-given nature and with the fundamental realities of the cosmos.

Secondly, that when God says, those who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day—along with the other attributes He assigns to them—this is intended to explain the rationale behind the command to fight them, while also giving the Muslims encouragement and motivation to do so.

Thirdly, that this refers to fighting the People of the Book altogether, not only some of them, as the preposition ‘from’ (min) in the phrase ‘from among those who were given the Book’ is for exposition (bayān) rather than division (tabʿīḍ).

As for the end of the verse: …until they pay the tribute (jizya) out of hand, being humbled (ṣāghirūn), al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says in his M ufradāt: ‘Jizya is the payment taken from the Protected Peoples (ahl al-dhimma). It is called jizya because it is given in repayment for their safety and legal protection.’ In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes:‘Jizya is a noun on the pattern of fiʿla that is derived from the verb jazā, yajzī (“to repay, to compensate”), like ʿiqda or jilsa, and it is a tax that they pay in recompense for their remaining disbelievers, as a penalty. This is narrated from ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā.’

Al-Rāghib’s interpretation appears more reliable because it is confirmed by what we have already said previously about jizya being a tax paid in return for their protection and the provision of services to them.

Al-Rāghib also says: ‘Ṣughr (smallness) and kibr (largeness) are relative opposites, where their usage always implies a comparison. For example, something might be small compared to one thing but large compared to something else… however, smallness (ṣighr) can also be used to denote abasement

(dhilla), equally one can be said to be ‘small’ (ṣāghir) if they are satisfied with a low station: …until they pay the tribute (jizya) out of hand (ʿan yad), being humbled (ṣāghirūn).’

Based on the attributes of the People of the Book that were mentioned at the beginning of the verse, which provided the rationale for fighting them, and the mention of them paying tribute in exchange for protection and security at its end, it appears that ‘humbled’ (ṣāghirūn) means that they have submitted themselves to the Islamic way of life and the just religious government

of Islamic society. Therefore, they will not compete with the M uslims for precedence in that society or oppose them by propagating their own desires in the form of their false doctrines and practices that are harmful to human society. At the same time, paying this tribute out of hand, as specified by the verse, symbolizes this inferiority.

Therefore, based on the apparent meaning of the verse, the meaning of humbled is not that the Muslims or the agents of the religious government should humiliate or mock them, for this is utterly beneath the dignity of Islam, even if some commentators on the Qur’an have suggested this meaning. The word yad (‘hand’) literally denotes the human limb but can also refer to a person’s power or blessings. If the word ‘hand’ in until they pay the tribute out of hand is used in the literal sense, then this means: ‘until they pay the tribute out of their hand and into yours.’ If, on the other hand, it is used in the second sense, then this means: ‘until they pay the tribute because of your power and authority over them and they are humbled, meaning they are neither obstinate nor arrogant toward you.’

Therefore, the meaning of the full verse is as follows: ‘Fight the People of the Book, because they do not believe in God and the Last Day in a way that is acceptable to God and which has not deviated from the right path; nor do they forbid those things that Islam has forbidden because they are harmful to human society; nor do they follow a religion that is in harmony with the divinely instituted cosmic order of things. So, fight them and continue to fight them until you have cowed them and they submit to your authority and they pay you the financial tribute you impose upon them that is commensurate with their inferior status. Spend this tribute on providing them with security, maintaining their safety, and managing their affairs.’

(9:30) The Jews say, ‘Ezra is the son of Allah,’ and the Christians say, ‘Christ is the son of Allah.’ That is an opinion that they mouth, imitating (yuḍāhiʾūn) the opinions of the faithless of former times. May Allah assail them, where do they stray (yuʾfakūn)?

Muḍāhāt (‘imitation’) means to emulate or mimic something.

According to al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, ifk (‘straying’) refers to anything that has been diverted from its proper course. Hence, yuʾfakūn here means that they have been diverted in their beliefs from truth to falsehood.

The Jews say, ‘Ezra is the son of Allah’: The Arabic name for Ezra is ʿUzayr; its pronunciation changed when it entered Arabic. The same is true of Yeshua (Jesus), which became ʿĪsā, and Yochanan (John), which became Yaḥyā. Ezra was the reviver of the Jewish faith who gathered the books of the Torah and wrote them as a single book after they had been lost when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, conquered their land. He had destroyed their temple; burned their books; massacred their men; and enslaved their women, children, and the weak, and taken them back to Babylon, where they remained in captivity for close to a century. W hen Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon, Ezra went to him to intercede on behalf of his people. Because Cyrus held Ezra in some esteem, he allowed him to return with his people to their homeland and to reproduce the Torah for them. Historians say that this transpired around the year 457 B.C. So, the Torah compiled by Ezra spread amongst the Israelites. However, it was lost once again in around

161 B.C. when the Seleucid king Antiochus VI conquered their lands and persecuted them, razing their homes, burning their books, and massacring all who he could lay his hands upon.

In any case, the great service that Ezra performed for the Israelites meant that he was greatly revered and respected amongst them, to the extent that they called him ‘the Son of God.’ It is not clear whether they meant this in the same sense as the Christians did for Jesus— in the sense that he contained some substance of divinity, or that he was an emanation of God, or that he was one and the same as God—or whether this was merely a term of respect and veneration, as when they say: we are Allah’s sons and His beloved ones (5:18). However, the context of the following verse—They have taken their scribes and their monks as lords besides Allah, and also Christ, M ary’s son (9:31)—would seem to suggest the latter was the case, as we shall discuss.

Some commentators on the Qur’an have said that the claim that Ezra was the son of God was only made by some of the Jews at the time of the Prophet, not by all of them. Equally, it was only some Jews in Medina at the time of the Prophet who said: Allah is poor and we are rich (3:181); and Allah’s hand is tied up (5:64). However, God ascribes these words to them in general because there were others who tacitly approved of the word and deeds of others because, in reality, they were all of the same opinion and orientation.

… and the Christians say, ‘Christ is the son of Allah’: This is a doctrine of the Christians. We have already discussed this in our treatment of the story of Jesus in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān.

… imitating the opinions of the faithless of former times: This passage calls attention to the fact that their claim that Jesus was the son of God

mimicked the beliefs of earlier disbelieving nations who worshipped idols and who believed in some deities who were parents of others, such that there were fathers, mothers, husbands, wives, sons, and daughters amongst the gods. The same is true of the doctrine of the trinity, which bears a resemblance to the teachings of the polytheistic religions of ancient Egypt, India, and China. We have already discussed this in our commentary on the story of Jesus in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān.

We have also mentioned there how the beliefs of polytheists and idolaters found their way into the Christian and Jewish faiths, which is something the Qur’an alludes to in the present verse when it accuses them of imitating the opinions of the faithless of former times.

Many contemporary scholars have examined the influences of the Buddhist and Hindu faiths on the contents of the Tanakh (or Old Testament) and the New Testament, and they have found instances where the teachings of these scriptures follow those of Buddhism and Hinduism almost step-by-step—even many of the stories and parables contained in the New Testament. Therefore, no one can be in doubt that the Qur’an is accurate in its description of them as ‘im itating.’

Then the Qur’an closes the verse by invoking a prayer against them, May Allah assail them.

(9:31) They have taken their scribes (aḥbār) and their monks (ruhbān) as lords besides Allah, and also Christ, Mary’s son;

though they were commanded to worship only the One Allah, there is no Allah except Him; immaculate is He above the partners that they ascribe!

Aḥbār (‘scribes’) is the plural of ḥibr (also spelled ḥabr) and denotes a scholar; it is commonly used to denote Jewish scholars. Ruhbān (‘monks’) is the plural of rāhib and it refers to those who don robes of piety. It is commonly used to denote Christian ascetics.

W hen the Qur’an accuses the Jews and Christians of taking their scribes and monks as lords besides God, this means that they listen to them and obey them unquestioningly, when only God is worthy of such obedience.

As for their taking Jesus son of Mary as a lord besides God, this is because the Christians ascribe divinity to him in the way that is common to most Christian sects. The Qur’an refers to Jesus as the ‘son of M ary’ to emphasise his humanity and show the error of the Christians worshipping him as God when, in fact, he is a man born of a woman like any other.

Note the difference between the way in which the Jews and the Christians take their scribes and monks as lords besides God and the way in which the Christians take Jesus as a lord besides God. This is why the Qur’an has mentioned the two separately, beginning with the scribes and monks, then adding:

and also Christ, M ary’s son.

M oreover, in the same way that the verse indicates that there are two different conceptions of lordship (rubūbiyya) at work here, it highlights that there

are two different conceptions of divine sonship (bunuwwa) present as well: In the case of Ezra, this is meant as an honorary sonship (bunuwwa tashrīfiyya), whereas in the case of Jesus it is meant somewhat literally. This distinction is brought into view by the fact that the present verse accuses the Christians of turning Jesus into a lord besides God, but it does not do the same to the Jews with regard to Ezra, mentioning only that they took their scribes and monks as lords besides God.

Therefore, Ezra could only be a lord (rabb) in their eyes if this was implied by his being a ‘son of God’ or because he was a scribe and he had performed a virtually incomparable service to their faith by restoring it after it had been destroyed. As for Jesus, when the Christians refer to him as the ‘son of God,’ they mean this in a different sense entirely.

…though they were commanded to worship only one Allah: This sentence is adverbial, meaning: ‘They took them as lords even though they were

commanded to worship only the One Allah.’

This statement shows, first of all, that taking someone as a lord by obeying them is the same as taking someone as a lord by worshipping them. To

obey someone unquestioningly is to worship them, therefore, it follows that a lord who is obeyed absolutely and unconditionally is tantamount to a god (ilāh), for a god is one who is worshipped and who is worthy of worship. This is illustrated by the fact that God says, though they were commanded to worship only one Allah, which substitutes ‘lord’ (rabb) for ‘god.’ On the other hand, if there was a distinction between the two, it would have been more appropriate to say: ‘though they were commanded to take only one lord.’ This shows that taking someone as a lord by giving them your absolute obedience is the same as taking them as a lord by making them an object of worship, in both cases you are taking them as a deity besides God.

Second, it shows that when the Qur’an calls on people to worship God alone— for example, in the verses: There is no Allah except M e; so worship M e

(21:25); So do not invoke any Allah besides Allah (26:213); and others—this not only means to restrict worship (ʿibāda) to God in the conventional sense of the word, it also means to restrict obedience (ṭāʿa) to Him. This is evident from the Qur’an, because it rebukes them for their blind obedience to their scribes and monks by saying: though they were commanded to worship only one Allah, and nothing else.

This reading is further supported by the verse: Did I not exhort you, O children of Adam, saying: ‘Do not worship Satan. He is indeed your manifest enemy. Worship Me. That is a straight path’? (36:61). And behind this door lies a thousand others.

As for His saying: …there is no Allah except Him, this represents the completion of the message of the previous phrase, though they were commanded

to worship only one Allah, as even though the idol worshippers believed in the existence of a multitude of gods, some of them would only worship one of these. However, worshipping only one god is not monotheism unless you also believe that there is no god besides him.

Hence, this verse deals with both forms of worship at the same time while still acknowledging the differences between them. It also shows that the way in which human beings must submit to God is by dedicating both forms of worship to Him. For example, God commands His Prophet to summon the People of the Book to worship Him with the following: Say, ‘O People of the Book! Come to a word common between us and you: that we will worship no one but Allah, and that we will not ascribe any partner to Him, and that we will not take each other as lords besides Allah.’ But if they turn away, say, ‘Be witnesses that we are those who submit to Allah’ (3:64).

The coda of the verse, immaculate is He above the partners that they ascribe, declares that He is exalted above their claims of lordship for their scribes and monks, or indeed their associating Jesus with him as a partner in divinity. Therefore, the present verse serves as an explanation of the earlier statement, those who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day (9:29). After

all, the fact that they have taken a god or gods besides God is not compatible with truly believing in Him nor in believing in the Last Day, on which there will be no sovereignty besides God’s.

(9:32) They desire to put out (yuṭfiʾū) the light of Allah with their mouths (bi afwāhihim), but Allah is intent on perfecting His light though the faithless should be averse.

Yuṭfiʾū (‘to put out’) means to extinguish a light or a flame, and the preposition bi in bi afwāhihim (‘with their mouths’) signifies the means or the reason

by which they extinguish this light.

The verse mentions their mouths because people blow through their mouths in order to extinguish a lamp or candle. In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes: ‘This is an example of eloquent speech because it belittles them and exposes the feebleness of their efforts, as one can only afiect the weakest of lights with one’s mouth rather than great blazes.’

In al-Kashshāf, al-Zamakhsharī says: ‘Their efforts to refute the prophethood of Muḥammad through their denials are akin to someone trying to

extinguish a light that illuminates the horizon and that God wishes to increase so that it reaches its full brightness and brilliance by blowing on it.’ Therefore, the verse illustrates powerfully the condition of the Islamic mission at this point in history as well as what the faithless aimed to do to it. Likewise, the verse also contains a beautiful promise from God that He will complete His light in spite of their efforts.

(9:33) It is He who has sent His Messenger with the guidance (hudā) and the religion of truth (dīn al-ḥaqq), that He may make it prevail over all religions, though the polytheists should be averse. Hudā (‘guidance’) refers to the divine guidance that was sent down with the Messenger of God to guide mankind by God’s command; the dīn al-ḥaqq (‘religion of truth’) is Islam, insofar as the teachings and rules of Islam correspond to objective reality.

Hence, this verse means that God is the one who sent His Messenger— Muḥammad—with guidance—in the form of clear signs and manifest proofs—and the religion of human nature (fiṭra), that He might make His religion— which is the religion of truth— triumph over all other religions, even if the idol worshippers are averse to this.

Based on this, it is plain that the pronoun ‘it’ in the phrase ‘make it prevail’ refers to the religion of truth, which is also indicated by the context. Some commentators might suggest that the pronoun actually refers to the Prophet—as

in, ‘make him prevail’— in which case it would mean: ‘To make His Messenger victorious and educate him with all the teachings of the religion.’ However, this is an extremely unlikely meaning for the verse.

Together, this and the previous verse clearly encourage the faithful to fight the People of the Book and indicate that this is a religious duty they must carry out. Both verses show that God wishes this religion to spread to all mankind, and this requires effort and struggle. At the same time, the People of the Book wish to extinguish this divine light with their mouths, so there is no option but to fight them until they are no more or until they hasten to pay tribute and submit themselves. After all, God will not accept any outcome other than to complete His light, and He wants this religion to triumph over all religions. It is God’s will that the Muslims should triumph over their enemies. Therefore, they should not slacken or grieve, for they have the upper hand, if they are truly believers.

(9:34) O you who have faith! Indeed many of the scribes and monks wrongfully eat up the people’s wealth, and bar from the way of Allah. And those who treasure up gold and silver, and do not spend it in the way of Allah, give tidings to them of a painful punishment. It appears that this verse is an explanation of what was said at the beginning of this section: nor forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden,

nor practise the religion of truth (9:29), in the same way that the previous verse provided an explanation of the clause immediately before it: those who do not have faith in Allah nor in the Last Day.

This verse explains nor forbid what Allah and His M essenger have forbidden by saying: Indeed many of the scribes and monks wrongfully eat up the

people’s wealth. In doing so, it provides the most egregious and persuasive example of how they corrupt human society and undermine the goals of religion.

The Qur’an enumerates in detail the wrongdoings and misdeeds of the People of the Book, especially the Israelites, in Sūrah al-Baqarah, Sūrah al-Nisāʾ,

Sūrah al-Māʾida, and in its other chapters. However, wrongdoings and transgressions involving money have a special status, especially when discussing

how the People of the Book cause corruption in righteous human societies when they are given a free hand and able to do as they please, for there is no force of corruption greater than monetary transgressions.

This is because one of the most important foundations upon which the edifice of human society rests is that of the economy, which God has made a source of social stability. If we analyze the majority of crimes, transgressions, and injustices that people commit, they stem from one of two causes. The first is extreme poverty, which leads people to covet the wealth of others through theft, banditry, murder, cheating in the marketplace, usurping other’s property, and so on. The second is extreme wealth, which leads a person to spend

extravagantly on food, drink, clothing, accommodation, and marriage, to become consumed by their desires, overstep the bounds of decency, and to infringe on the life, property, and dignity of others.

Now, if we examine the different forms of corruption that step from these two extremes of wealth, we see that each of them has a negative impact on the system that manages the acquisition and ownership of property, and on the laws promulgated to distinguish between licit and illicit ways of consuming wealth. If this system of ownership breaks down, then people allow themselves to claim whatever property they can lay their hands on and accumulate

wealth by any way possible, regardless of whether or not it is right for them to do so. Equally, they will look to satisfy their every self sh whim and desire without regard to its morality or lack thereof, no matter the consequences of this. This, in turn, generates a crisis of corruption in society and the spread of moral decadence. Society is transformed from a human environment to a base animal one that is governed solely by the stomach and whatever lies beneath it. In such a society, no one has any interest in politics or education, and no one gives any thought to wisdom or heeds any moral warnings.

Perhaps this is why God singles out embezzling people’s wealth for mention here, especially when this is done by the scribes and monks who are supposed to be sources of moral education for their people and agents of reform

in society.

Some have explained that the monks and scribes embezzled wealth by taking the money people donated to them because of their appearance of piety and asceticism, by charging usury, gaining wealth by illicit means, confiscating their opponents’ property, or taking bribes as judges, and by selling

indulgences or certificates that promised the bearer entry into heaven. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it refers to their taking bribes as judges, as we have already discussed in our commentary on the verse: O M essenger! Do not grieve for those who are active in unfaith (5:41). And, even if this were not the case and the verse was only referring to the practice of the Church in selling indulgences, this by itself would be sufficiently abhorrent to merit such condemnation.

As for the idea that this wealth was given to them in the form of donations because of their asceticism and piety, or in the form of pious endowments, wills, and bequests, this does not count as wrongfully eating up people’s wealth. Equally, God has attributed usury and earning wealth illicitly to the People of the Book in general, and not only their clergy: and for their taking usury—though they had been forbidden from it—and for eating up the wealth of the people wrongfully (4:161), and Eavesdroppers with the aim of telling lies, eaters of the unlawful (5:42), whereas, in the present verse, God is concerned with the wrongdoing that is specific to the scribes and monks. Therefore, God’s condemnation of their embezzlement of people’s wealth is not a condemnation of something that includes the ordinary people.

It is the spiritual leaders of a community and their religious scholars who are supposed to teach them how to worship God and encourage them to reform their hearts and their deeds. W hen these individuals go astray and abandon the path of truth for that of falsehood, the truth is that whatever livelihood they earn or benefits they acquire after this are ill-gotten and illicit,

and forbidden to them by both reason and religion.

Returning to the verse at hand, it also explains nor practise the religion of truth (9:29) by saying: and bar from the way of Allah. This is also based on the three attributes that God ascribed to them previously, the third of which is that they do not practise the religion of truth. This explains how their attributes and their deeds harm human society and impede the aims of the just religious government, namely to bring about moral reform in people and create a society that is alive and fiourishing in a way that agrees with the human being’s

innate nature (fiṭra) and directs him towards his natural happiness (saʿāda). This is why, out of all the various vices that He could mention, God singles out the fact that they do not practise the religion of truth, because it is the most

destructive to human society: They use all of their powers and expend whatever resources they have, both apparent and hidden, to bar others from the

way of God and prevent them from following it, and they have been doing this since the time of the Prophet down to the present day.

As for His saying, and those who treasure up (yaknizūn) gold and silver, and do not spend it in the way of Allah, give tidings to them of a painful punishment, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī says: ‘Kanz (“to treasure up”) means to pile coins

on top of one another and hoard them. It originally meant to store dates in a container; the kannāz season is the time of year in which dates are stored. At the same time, a camel is called kannāz when it has been fattened up. As for the verse, and those who treasure up gold and silver, this means that they hoard them.’

Therefore, the use of the word kanz conveys the idea of hoarding wealth and preventing it from flowing freely between people in various kinds of dealings. Such a movement of wealth from one person to another would allow

it to grow in a way that was beneficial not only to individuals but to society as a whole. Before the emergence of banks and treasuries, people would bury their hoarded treasure in the ground to keep it safe from those who would seek to deprive them of it.

Textually speaking, this verse is connected to the previous verses that criticise the People of the Book and rebuke their scribes and monks for devouring

people’s wealth falsely and barring others from the way of God. However, it contains no indication whatsoever in its wording that it was revealed about them alone or that its meaning was specific to them. Therefore, one cannot argue that this verse only applies to the People of the Book and that they are forbidden from hoarding wealth but that Muslims are free to pile up gold and silver and do with their property as they please without compunction. On the contrary, this verse delivers a stern warning to those who hoard their wealth and threatens them with a severe punishment. However, the verse also clarifies what is condemnable about those who treasure up gold and silver, namely that they do not spend it in the way of Allah. Therefore, what God detests about hoarding is when it leads a person to not spend his wealth in His way when he is confronted with an opportunity to do so.

Based on what we read in the Qur’an, the way of God (sabīl Allāh) refers to whatever the religion of God depends upon for its security and stability. For example: waging jihād, protecting the essential interests of the religion, looking after the social affairs of Muslims without which society would collapse, and paying one’s religious dues through which the religion strengthens

the foundations of the religious community. Therefore, those who treasure up gold and silver while there are essential needs not being met have hoarded their wealth and not spent it in the way of God. Those people, God says, should be given tidings of a painful punishment, for they have given preference to themselves over their Lord and placed their own needs or those of potential future

of spring before the very real and present needs of the religious community. This can also be understood from the contents of the next verse, especially the line which reads: This is what you treasured up for yourselves! (9:35).

There, God rebukes them for keeping their wealth to themselves because they feared they might one day need it rather than spending it in God’s way, which is the very lifeblood of human society in both this world and the Hereafter. And, in doing so, they have also betrayed God and His Messenger in another way: through concealing their wealth and keeping it hidden. Had they made known their wealth and allowed it to flow freely, perhaps the one in authority would have told them to spend it for a particularly pressing religious cause. However, because they hoarded their wealth and kept it hidden from others, the one in authority did not say anything about it, so the urgent need was not met as a result. In other words, there was hoarded wealth sitting idle when it was the one way to alleviate this need, while the one who hoarded it had no need of it at that time.

Therefore, the verse only condemns people for amassing wealth when this means that they prefer to keep it for themselves when they have no need of it instead of spending it in the way of God when there is an urgent need to do so. The reader should not imagine that Islam limits the right of ownership to a certain quantity of wealth. On the contrary, someone might have vast quantities of gold and silver but, instead of treasuring them up, makes use of them.

Had the person who hoarded his wealth done this, he would have benefited from many times over, while also benefitting others through buying and selling, through employing others, through investing, or through some other

means. In any case, someone who makes use of their wealth is not subject to this religious prohibition, because instead of trying to keep it hidden from others, he has used this wealth in a way that promotes economic growth and brings benefit to himself and others. He has not concealed it or prevented it from being used in the way of God. In fact, even if he doesn’t spend it in the way of God, this condemnation still does not apply to him, because the ruler of the Muslims can always command him to spend in God’s way as he seems necessary. Therefore, even if he does not spend in God’s way, so long as he makes no attempt to conceal his wealth, he is neither a traitor nor a wrongdoer. On the contrary, the verse in question only concerns hoarded wealth whose owner avoids paying his religious dues from it. This is not only in the sense of obligatory religious taxes, rather it includes both them and any urgent need that religious society has, such as waging jihād, saving lives, or the like thereof.

There are also recommended (mustaḥabb) ways of spending in the way of God, such as spending it on one’s dependants or giving it to poor persons to use for something more than their basic needs. However, while these fall within the category of ‘spending in the way of God,’ the same evidences that show they are recommended reveal that they are not what is meant by ‘spending in the way of God’ in the verse under discussion. Keeping one’s wealth

and not spending it on something recommended in the absence of something necessary to spend it is not the kind of ‘treasuring up’ that is forbidden by the verse, as can be seen from the verse itself.

Lengthy theological debates have also taken place amongst commentators regarding this verse, and we will address these after our discussion of the

narrations relating to the current section of verses.

When God says, give tidings to them of a painful punishment, this is an explicit threat of punishment, which shows the severity of the prohibition.

(9:35) on the day when these shall be heated (yuḥmā ʿalayhā) in hellfire and therewith branded (tukwā bihā) on their foreheads, their sides and their backs: ‘This is what you treasured up for yourselves! So taste what you have treasured!’

The verb iḥmāʾ (‘to heat’) means to make something hot enough to cause a person discomfort, and when it is made transitive with the preposition ʿalā (lit. ‘upon’) it means to light a fire upon something until it becomes hot. Kawā—from which the verb takwā (‘to brand or cauterise’) is derived—means to press something hot against a body.

Therefore, the verse means: ‘That painful punishment you are to give them tidings of is that those treasures will be heated in the fires of hell until they become burning hot. Then they will be pressed into the foreheads, sides, and backs of those who hoarded them. Then they will be told: “This is what you treasured up for yourselves! So taste what you have treasured!” for those treasures have become a source of punishment for them in the Hereafter.’ Note that God specifically mentions their forehead, sides, and backs. This might be symbolic: For example, they lowered and abased themselves for these treasures, and one prostrates with one’s forehead; they sought shelter with them, and one seeks shelter with one’s side; and they relied on them, and one leans on something with one’s back.

(22) In the same source, al-Suyūṭī narrates from Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abī Shayba, al-Bukhārī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh, who narrate from Zayd b. Wahb, who said: ‘I came upon Abū Dharr in al-Rabadha and asked him: ‘What brought you to this remote place?’

(23) In the same source, it is narrated from M uslim and Ibn M ardawayh from al-Aḥnafib. Qays: ‘Abū Dharr came and said: “Give tidings to those who treasure up wealth that they will be branded on their backs, and it will burn through to their sides and branded on their foreheads, and it will burn through to the back of their heads!” I said: “What is that?” He said: “I did not tell them anything save what I heard their Prophet say.”’

‘Then he turned away from the group and went and sat down to one side. I followed him and sat next to him without having any idea who he was. Do you see this mountain of Uḥud?” I said: “Yes.” He said: “I would love to have a pile of gold the size of this mountain so that I could give it all away save for three dinars. They do not understand that they are only gathering provisions for this world. By God, I will not ask them for anything of this world nor ask them questions about religion until I meet God Almighty.”’

(26) In the Taʾrīkh of al-Ṭabarī, it is related from Shuʿayb, from Sayf, from Muḥammad b. ʿAwf, from ʿIkrama, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Abū Dharr went to ʿUthmān while Kaʿb al-Aḥbār was with him and told ʿUthmān: ‘You should not be content with people not harming one another until they also give charitably to one another, for it might befit the giver of zakāt not to restrict himself to zakāt alone but also to give charitably to his neighbours, his brethren, and include his relatives also.’

Kaʿb replied: ‘Whoever does what is obligatory has discharged his duty and need not do anything more.’

At this, Abū Dharr took his crook and struck him on the head, wounding him and exposing his skull.

ʿUthmān pleaded with him to stop, and Abū Dharr did. He said: ‘O Abū Dharr, fear God and control your hand and your tongue!’ For when Abū Dharr struck him, he had said: ‘O son of a Jewish woman , what are you talking about?’

Author’s comments: The stories of Abū Dharr and his disagreements with ʿUthmān and Muʿāwiya are well known and recorded in the books of Taʾrīkh. Reflecting on the content of the above traditions and, in particular, what Abū Dharr said to Muʿāwiya, this suggests that this verse was not understood as only applying to the People of the Book. Furthermore, his altercation with ʿUthmān and Kaʿb suggests that our reading of the verse is correct,

namely that its threat of punishment is directed to those who do not spend in obligatory cases in addition to zakāt.

Our reading is further supported by an analysis of how people lived at that time. Looking at history, we find that people then were divided into two broad groups: a majority who struggled to subsist from day-to-day and barely had enough to clothe themselves and meet their essential needs; and a minority who had become intoxicated with the world and amassing the wealth and

property it contained. They amassed millions upon millions of dinars and dirhams in gifts from rulers, the spoils of war, and the taxation of land. It is enough for you to refer to the chronicles that recorded the fabulous wealth of some of the Companions; they owned large sums of money, slaves, estates, and mansions. In Syria, Muʿāwiya and the Umayyad Dynasty managed to create a court that was at least comparable in its luxury to those of the Roman

and Persian emperors.

However, Islam does not approve of such extreme differences in wealth unless those with it spend on those without it to narrow the gap between the social classes, for the general situation must be remedied by the wealthy showing compassion to the poor and the strong to the weak.

Now, one might say: Abū Dharr merely expressed his own scholarly understanding (ijtihād) that any wealth in excess of what is needed to feed and clothe oneself is a treasure or hoard (kanz) that must be spent in the way of God. Or, one might say: He was calling people to practice asceticism in regard to worldly things.

However, the reports of what he said fiatly contradict this hypothesis. Abū Dharr does not say anything that would indicate this was his personal opinion or individual understanding as a scholar. On the contrary, he says: ‘I did not tell them anything save what I heard their Prophet say,’ or ‘My friend said such-and-such.’ Furthermore, there are narrations with sound (ṣaḥīḥ) chains of transmitters that are found in both Sunnī and Shīʿī collections, in which the Prophet said: ‘There is no one under the heavens or upon the earth more honest in speech than Abū Dharr.’

This refutes the statement of Shaddād b. Aws, which has been narrated from him by Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and al-Ṭabarānī: ‘Abū Dharr would hear a ruling from the Messenger of God and go out to his tribe of Bedouins. However,

the Messenger of God would later explain the ruling in such a way that showed it to be less stringent than it had first seemed. Everyone else preserved the lessstringent version of the ruling given by the Messenger of God, but Abū Dharr

did not hear it, because he was absent, so he acted on the more stringent version he had initially heard.’

However, Abū Dharr’s claim that the verse about treasuring up wealth

(9:34) is not restricted to the People of the Book but includes both them and the Muslims is not an example of what the above report ascribes to him, namely that he would take the more stringent ruling (ʿazīma) over the less stringent one (rukhṣa). Neither is his statement that merely paying the zakāt is not sufficient to remove the prohibition on hoarding wealth so long as a person is not spending on what is obligatory in the way of God. It is inconceivable that Abū Dharr did not hear the Messenger of God say that there are

two kinds of charity, obligatory and recommended, or that he did not know that the evidences for supererogatory charity provide the best clarification for the scope of the verse on hoarding wealth.

Weaker than Shaddād’s narration is what al-Ṭabarī relates in his Taʾrīkh from Shuʿayb, from Sayf, from ʿAṭiyya, from Yazīd al-Faqaʿsī: When Ibn al-Sawdāʾ came to Syria, he met Abū Dharr and said: ‘Are you not amazed by Muʿāwiya saying: “All wealth belongs to God. Lo! Surely everything belongs to God!” It is as though he wants to keep it for himself to the exclusion of the M uslims and erase the name “M uslims” from the fiscal registers altogether!’ So Abū Dharr went to Muʿāwiya and said: ‘How can you call the wealth of the Muslims “the wealth of God”?’

He answered: ‘God have mercy on you, Abū Dharr! Are we not God’s servants? Is not all wealth God’s wealth? Is not all creation His? Is not all command His?’

Abū Dharr said: ‘Do not use this expression!’

Muʿāwiya said: ‘I will not say that it does not belong to God, but henceforth I will call it “the wealth of the Muslims.”’

Then Ibn al-Sawdāʾ went to Abū al-Dardāʾ and said: ‘Who are you? By God, I think you are a Jew!’ Then ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit came and seized him, took him to Muʿāwiya, and said: ‘This is the one who is always provoking Abū Dharr against you!’

Abū Dharr got up in Syria and began to speak: ‘O men of wealth, show kindness to the poor. Give tidings to those who treasure up gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah of branding irons from a fire with which they will be branded on their foreheads, their sides and their backs!’ According to this account, Abū Dharr only took this stance and protested at the urging of Ibn al-Sawdāʾ, and the two sources from whom al-Ṭabarī narrates this report and the bulk of his material about ʿUthmān—Shuʿayb and

Sayf— are known liars and fabricators of traditions, as is clearly recorded by scholars of narrators’ biographies (rijāl). They have likewise fabricated traditions from Ibn al-Sawdāʾ, who is also known by the name ʿAbd Allāh b. Sabaʾ,

and researchers have established that Ibn Sabaʾ is a purely fictional personality without a historical basis.

(27) In al-Durr al-M anthūr, it is narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from Jābir that the Messenger of God said: ‘There is no hoarder of wealth who does not pay what is due from it save that on the Day of Judgement he will be taken and branded on his forehead and his sides and told:

“This is the treasure with which you were stingy!”’

(28) In the same source, it is narrated from al-Ṭabarānī’s al-Awsaṭ and Abū Bakr al-Shāfiʿī’s Ghaylāniyyāt from ʿAlī that the Messenger of God said: ‘Surely God has imposed a duty on wealthy Muslims concerning their wealth, as much as sufiices the poor, and the poor will never suffer from hunger or poverty except for the fact that the wealthy refrain from giving in charity. Lo! Surely God will hold the wealthy to account most severely or punishment them most painfully because of this!’

(29) In the same source, it is narrated by al-Ḥākim, who considers it sound (ṣaḥīḥ, and by al-Dhahabī, who considers it weak (ḍaʿīf), from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, from Bilāl, that the Messenger of God told him: ‘O Bilāl, meet God as a beggar and do not meet him as a wealthy person!’ Bilāl asked: ‘How can I do that?’ He said: ‘If you are given sustenance (rizq), do not conceal it, and if someone asks you for charity, do not refuse them.’ Bilāl asked: ‘How can I do that?’ He said: ‘It is just as I said, or else it is hellfire.’

A Discussion on the Meaning of ‘Hoard’ or ‘Treasure’ (Kanz)

There is no doubt that the communities that human beings form according to their innate nature exist for the purpose of exchanging goods and services with one another. Were this not the case, human communities would

not last for the blink of an eye. A person benefits from being part of a community as follows: They work on the raw materials of the earth to the best

of their ability in order to provide for their own needs and, in doing so, they produce a surplus. They then take this surplus and exchange it with other members of the community in order to acquire other things that they need but cannot produce for themselves. For example, a baker makes enough bread for himself and then exchanges the rest for a garment made by a tailor. This is how members of a community engage in trade and barter with one another in order to meet their needs.

Economic research has shown that members of primitive societies would exchange one thing for another without paying attention to anything else. However, not all things could be exchanged equally, because people had need of some goods more than others, and some goods are more abundant and readily available than others, while others were harder to obtain. So, the greater

peoples’ need was for something or the harder it was to obtain, the more demand there was for it, which rendered it more valuable relative to other goods. Conversely, the less people needed something or the more abundantly it was available, the less demand existed for it and, as a result, its value relative

to other goods decreased. This is the economic basis of price.

Then, certain highly prized goods were adopted as a medium of exchange, in relation to which the values of all other goods, such as wheat, eggs, or salt, were determined and quantified. These goods then became the basis around which markets revolved, and this economic model can be seen at work in small communities today, for example in villages or amongst Bedouin tribes. This state of affairs continued until people acquired precious metals such as gold, silver, copper and the like thereof, which they made the basis for measuring the value of all items. As such, they provided a standardised measure

of value: Gold was the most valuable, followed by silver, followed by other metals. All of these metals were then minted into coins by various kingdoms and states, so that they became dinars, dirhams, fils, and so on. However, to discuss the origins of money further would take us beyond the scope of our present discussion.

In any case, it was not long before gold and silver currency became the standard on which everything was based, the measure of value for all goods or services, the axis of all of life’s needs, and the thing upon which wealth and prosperity depended. They became the essence of social life, such that any disruption in the flow of currency led to the disruption of society as a whole. They flowed through the markets and the markets flowed because of them. I have already explained the role assigned to them by human societies with regards to regulating the value of goods and services and providing means to compare the value of different things. The paper currency that circulates today in the form of pounds and dollars, as well as cheques, represents the value of things without actually having any value in of itself. Therefore, they are a pure representation of value that is abstracted from any actual commodity. As currencies, gold and silver perform an important societal function of regulating prices and providing an objective measure of value for different goods and services relative to one another. Reflecting on this, we see that

they actually represent the ratio between one thing and another, and insofar as they represent the ratios between things— or, if you will, they are the very ratios themselves— then all of these ratios would be invalidated if the currency was invalidated, and any stagnation in currency would necessarily lead to a stagnation in goods and services.

In fact, between the two World Wars of the twentieth century, we saw the effects of some currencies losing their value entirely, such as the Ruble in Tsarist Russia or the Mark in Germany. Both of these countries were plunged into deep crises as a result of economic stagnation and infiation that resulted from the devaluing of their currencies. Economic calamities such as this can also be caused by people hoarding wealth and impeding the free flow of currency amongst the population.

This is something highlighted in the previously quoted tradition from Imām al-Bāqir, which is narrated by Shaykh al-Ṭūsī in his Amālī: ‘He created (gold and silver) for the benefit of His creatures, that they might organise their affairs and meet their needs with them.’

Hence, it is clear that hoarding money is economically equivalent to devaluing commodities, as it hoarding money is rendered inert and unproductive.

After all, if this money was not being sequestered away but was circulating through the economy instead, then it would be stimulating the market and facilitating transactions, with the beneficial effects of both of these being felt throughout society. Rendering money inert is akin to closing down the market, which is akin to stopping the very lifeblood of society, as stagnation in

the market leads to stagnation and decline in society.

Now, when I say, ‘hoarding money,’ I do not mean merely keeping it in treasuries or secure locations, for all human beings know instinctively that it is both good sense and a moral duty to protect one’s wealth and valuables from loss or theft. W henever money is invested in any sort of business venture and comes back to its owner, it is obligatory for them to protect this wealth from loss, theft, fraud, or embezzlement. Instead, by ‘hoarding money,’ what I mean is to keep it apart from the flow of market transactions and prevent it from circulating through the various areas of economic life in which it is used to meet the needs of society, such as feeding the hungry, quenching the thirsty, clothing the naked, generating profits, benefitting workers, growing capital, treating the sick, freeing captives, helping debtors, helping those in distress, preserving the security of a righteous society, and reforming those areas of it that have been corrupted.

These areas of spending—whether the spending itself is considered obligatory, recommended, or permissible—are too many to count, and a person

should not go to either of the extremes of stinginess or wastefulness in any of them. However, while there is nothing sinful about not spending on recommended causes from the perspective of either reason or religion, seeking

to dismiss the importance of recommended cases of spending as a category altogether is, in fact, the worst sort of crime or sin.

Consider your own daily life and the various areas of it on which you spend, whether on your home, your spouse, your food and drink, or your clothes, and think about what would happen if you spent your money only on what was absolutely ‘necessary’— namely that which religiously obligatory—what kind of life would that be? If you avoided any kind of ‘unnecessary’ spending (in the broadest sense of the word), your life would be damaged

beyond all repair.

Based on the above explanation, when God says, and those who treasure up gold and silver, and do not spend it in the way of Allah, give tidings to them of a painful punishment (9:34), it does not seem at all unlikely that He has in mind spending on the kind of recommended things we have already discussed, as ‘treasuring up’ wealth goes against not only obligatory but also recommended spending as a matter of principle.

This also clarifies the meaning of what Abū Dharr said to ʿUthmān b.

ʿAfiān when he went to see him according to al-Ṭabarī’s narration, namely: ‘You should not be content with people not harming one another until they also give charitably to one another, for it might befit the giver of zakāt not to restrict himself to zakāt alone but also to give charitably to his neighbors, his brethren, and include his relatives also.’ He explicitly states that he does not consider it obligatory for a person to give away all of their excess wealth so long as zakāt had been paid; he also drew a clear distinction between obligatory and recommended cases of spending in the way of God. However, what

he reportedly found objectionable was the idea that no charity was necessary beyond the obligatory, which efiectively closes the door on all manner of good deeds, undermines the very aims of Islam’s legislation on charity, and is harmful to the public interest.

In other words, he is saying: ‘This is not a dictatorship like that of Rome or Persia, which has no duty to its people except to maintain security and stability by preventing people from harming one another and that people are then free to do as they please and even to go to any extremes they desire, to be moral or immoral, to follow guidance or go astray, and—like their own government—to not be held accountable by anyone!’

By contrast, the government of a religious society is not satisfied with people not harming one another. Instead, it directs people to what is best for them in all areas of life and works to promote happiness for all members of that society, whether they are rulers or ruled, leaders or led, served or serving, wealthy or poor, strong or weak. Such that the poor fulfil the needs of the rich through their labour and the rich fulfil the needs of the poor through their wealth; the position of the strong is preserved through the respect of the weak and the life of the weak is protected through the kindness and protection of the strong; the authority of the elite is maintained through the obedience of ordinary folk, while the obedience of ordinary folk is maintained through the justice and equanimity of the elite. However, none of this can be achieved except through the promotion of charity and good deeds in society; so that both obligatory and recommended duties will be performed according to what is appropriate for each. As for only giving what is obligatory and refusing to spend on recommended causes as a rule, this will devastate the very

foundation of religious life in society, undermine the aims of the Lawgiver, and quickly give rise to dysfunction, disruption, and deeply rooted corruption in the social order to the point of inevitable collapse. All of this emanates

from being lax in promoting the aims of the religion and being amicable with oppressors and tyrants.

This is why in al-Ṭabarī’s account, Abū Dharr said to Muʿāwiya, ‘How can you call the wealth of the Muslims “the wealth of God”?’

To which Muʿāwiya replied, ‘May God have mercy on you, Abū Dharr!

Are we not God’s servants? Is not all wealth God’s wealth? Is not all creation His? Is not all command His?’

And Abū Dharr told him, ‘Do not use this expression!’

This is because even if the expression that Muʿāwiya, his stooges, and the Umayyad caliphs who came after him used was true in its literal sense— and there are narrations from the Prophet and verses from the Qur’an that say as much—they had twisted its meaning to the opposite of what God had intended by it. The original meaning of everything being ‘the wealth of God’ was that it did not truly belong to anyone by virtue of their strength, authority, or power. Rather, it belonged to God and, therefore, they should spend it in His way for those causes He had specified. If it was something that a private individual had acquired through earnings, inheritance, or the like, then there was a rule for this. Equally, if it was something that the Islamic government had collected in the form of war spoils, tribute, land tax, charity, or the like thereof, then the religion has also specified the causes on which this can be spent. The holder of authority (walī al-amr) has no right to set aside any of that for himself or for a member of his family beyond what is necessary for their subsistence, let alone to hoard it, erect palaces, seclude themselves from their people, and live a life akin to that of a Roman or Persian emperor. So the Umayyad dynasty used the slogan that ‘all wealth is God’s wealth’ to ward of  people’s criticisms for misappropriating the wealth of the M uslims and spending it to satisfy their own self sh desires and in a manner that was contrary to God’s wishes. W hen those who were entitled to this wealth objected that they were squandering the wealth of the M uslims, they retorted, ‘All wealth is God’s wealth, and we have been entrusted it by Him to use however we see fit.’ In this way, they sought to justify their misappropriation of

God’s wealth and validate their misuse of it for their own personal benefit. In fact, their slogan means the opposite of what they claimed, because ‘God’s wealth’ and ‘the Muslims’ wealth’ mean the same thing, while Muʿāwiya and the Umayyads treated these as two separate categories and used one to invalidate the other.

If, when Muʿāwiya had said, ‘All wealth is God’s wealth,’ he had done so with its true meaning in mind, there would have been no sense in Abū Dharr storming out of his meeting with him and calling out: ‘Give tidings to those who treasure up gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah of branding irons from a fire with which they will be branded on their foreheads, their sides and their backs!’

After all, Muʿāwiya had told Abū Dharr that he thought the verse on hoarding wealth only applied to the People of the Book. Perhaps this was also why they had plotted to erase the ‘and’ from the beginning of the phrase, and those who treasure up gold and silver (9:34) when they were copying out ʿUthmān’s codex, which is also why—per the aforementioned narration—Abū Dharr threatened to fight them.

Therefore, even though the account that al-Ṭabarī reports from Sayfiand Shuʿayb appears to have been framed in a way to suggest that Abū Dharr was mistaken in his views—as al-Ṭabarī himself admits at the beginning of the account— there are elements in the story that ring true.

In short, then, the verse shows that it is forbidden to hoard gold and silver when there are urgent causes in the way of God on which it must be spent, or to refuse to give it to those who are entitled to zakāt, or to refuse to spend it on defending the community. Equally, it shows that it is forbidden to bar the way of voluntary good deeds and performing recommended acts of charity amongst the people.

Furthermore, it makes no difference to the ruling whether the wealth in question is visible and flowing through the marketplaces or whether it is treasure buried beneath the earth. The term kanz (‘treasure or hoard’) applies to

any excess wealth and the act of hoarding it and keeping it hidden is a crime against the rightful authority, as we have already discussed above.
